This study introduces a novel particle-based representation for sim-to-real robot manipulation of unfamiliar objects. A key advantage of this approach lies in its ability to process complex, unseen objects using minimal training data and visual information. A proposed method, called Degrading Convolutional Message Passing (DCMP), first generates a set of particles based on an image input and encodes the object's shape, pose, and self-contact. These particles are then transformed into a graph structure, where the nodes represent object parts and edges signify contact between particles. A tailored message-passing neural network is employed to integrate spatial relationships among particles, resulting in a more accurate prediction of the optimal grasp. Our approach demonstrates superior performance in grasping novel objects compared to alternative methods, as evidenced by experiments on a synthetic Dexterity Robotics gripper and a real-world R5 robot. Additionally, we show that our algorithm outperforms existing private prediction methods in both classification and regression tasks, as well as when using different privacy mechanisms, such as the Gaussian mechanism and random noise. Our work provides a comprehensive framework for private prediction, enabling the combination of different privacy mechanisms seamlessly. This research introduces a novel decentralized approach to designing controllers for networks of interconnected multi-agent systems. Drawing inspiration from traditional decentralized control methods, our strategy employs a network-wide consensus mechanism, utilizing a shared parameter to determine individual controller parameters. We demonstrate that a custom-designed linear time-invariant plant can be accurately replicated through decentralized control, with an associated error that diminishes as the network grows and the number of agents increases. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the network's structural properties play a crucial role in determining the ultimate achievable level of control accuracy. To illustrate the efficacy of our method, a simulation-based case study is presented. We propose that our decentralized control strategy has the potential to facilitate robust and efficient control of complex multi-agent systems. This work is part of an ongoing series, detailed in arXiv:2104.00060, where a centralized control design is initially considered, followed by an investigation of decentralized estimation, and finally, this developed decentralized control approach. Supporting materials, including code, can be found on the corresponding GitHub repository. A second part of this study, focusing on decentralized control over a decentralized estimator, is also available in arXiv:2201.10561. Our approach is related to the distributed control strategy presented in arXiv:2106.13493. However, our work differs in that it does not rely on explicit communication of the plant's parameters or state variables, nor does it require a centralized estimator. Instead, our strategy is grounded in a decentralized estimation approach, where local estimators produce estimates that are shared with neighboring agents to facilitate accurate control. We establish that the network's structural properties play a vital role in determining the overall system's performance. Furthermore, our research reveals that the network's structure is a key factor in mitigating the impact of communication delays, as demonstrated in simulations. Finally, our study explores the robustness of our decentralized control strategy when faced with communication uncertainties. Deep learning model training is typically carried out by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in combination with back-propagation. This process utilizes a mini-batch of data to estimate the cost function, allowing the model's parameters to be adjusted accordingly. However, the choice of batch size is a significant factor, as it affects the accuracy and efficiency of the learning process. Our research reveals that an optimal batch size exists, such that increasing it beyond this point yields the same learning outcome as its corresponding batch size equivalent. This finding holds true for various cost functions, including quadratic, cross-entropy, and others, as proven by mathematical theorems and supported by computational experiments. Consequently, our results indicate that employing a larger batch size does not necessarily result in faster SGD convergence, and we confirm this phenomenon through a series of numerical simulations. Moreover, our study investigates the impact of the batch size on the convergence time of SGD, providing insights into its behavior in relation to the cost function, the model's degree of over-complexity, and the data distribution. Notably, the optimal batch size proves to be particularly significant in deep learning, where it diverges from the results obtained in the linear setting. Our research also explores the interplay between the batch size and the learning rate, revealing a connection between the two, as well as their respective effects on the model's performance. Finally, our study includes a practical application, demonstrating the potential to increase the model's capacity without compromising the model's performance by employing a larger batch size. This has the added benefit of significantly reducing the memory requirements, as the model's gradients are calculated using a batch size equivalent to the total data size. This achievement is particularly noteworthy, as it enables the training of large-scale models on devices with limited memory, such as smartphones, and we demonstrate this feasibility through a simulation of a VGG-16 model trained on a Google Pixel 4a. A key challenge in model training is efficiently transferring knowledge from a high-capacity model to a lower-capacity one. A widely-used method, knowledge distillation, has seen success in various applications but its underlying reasons for success remain unclear. This paper investigates the effectiveness of knowledge distillation by analyzing its connection to the mutual information between input features and labels. Our analysis reveals that the mutual information between these features is maximized when labels are most informative and features are most relevant. Contrary to previous assumptions, we found that the label similarity and similarity among features during the training process are not essential for successful knowledge distillation. Instead, we found that the features of the teacher model are actually more informative than those of the student model, allowing for more accurate predictions. Based on these findings, we developed a new approach to knowledge distillation that targets the mutual information between features and labels. Our method was able to improve the performance of the student model without the need for temperature adjustment or label smoothing. In fact, it was able to surpass the performance of the teacher model without the need for extensive training. Additionally, our method was able to improve the performance of the student model when the teacher model was not well-suited to the training data. Our method's effectiveness was verified on various datasets and tasks, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and language modeling. The code for our method is available online. Our analysis and experimental results provide valuable insights into the underlying reasons for the success of knowledge distillation. The source code of our method is available online. The experiments were conducted using the Mini-ImageNet and CUB datasets. Our results indicate that the generative model outperforms standard meta-learning approaches, and we observe that the generated data proves challenging for the model, suggesting that it is learning from the data and not just adapting to it. In microfluidic systems, a device's design plays a significant role in determining the direction and speed of a solute's transport in a channel. While diffusion is typically the primary driving force, there are certain conditions under which other effects can take precedence. Diffusi-phytic transport is characterized by the competition between diffusion and buoyancy, resulting in a unique distribution of solute that can be intentionally controlled. In this study, a novel approach to creating diffusi-phytic devices is presented, leveraging the inherent differences in diffusion rates between solute and a solvating agent to produce a desired distribution. Specifically, a device is engineered to concentrate the solvating agent at the channel's edges, creating a diffusi-phytic effect that relies on solvation to direct the solute towards the center of the channel. Theoretical and numerical analyses, as well as experimental validation, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in enhancing solute transport. Furthermore, it is shown that this design concept can be easily adapted to facilitate the separation of solutes based on their ability to form complexes with the solvating agent, as demonstrated in a study involving the use of a fluorescent tag. The results of this study have significant implications for the development of novel microfluidic devices that can be used to analyze and sort particles at the microscale. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the interactions between diffusion, solvation, and complexation in microfluidic systems. Automated microscopes generate vast electron microscopy datasets, necessitating 
efficient analysis tools to extract meaningful insights. However, the sheer volume 
and complexity of the data pose significant challenges to developing practical 
algorithms for processing and reconstructing the data within reasonable time frames. 
In this research, we introduce a novel, accelerated approach to electron microscopy 
reconstruction, leveraging a combination of optimized data structures and accelerated 
linear algebra operations. Our implementation demonstrates substantial speedup, 
potentially enabling reconstruction times in minutes instead of days. Furthermore, 
we discuss potential applications and future directions that could further enhance 
the algorithm's efficiency. Our code, designed for compatibility with existing 
reconstruction methods, is freely available and aims to facilitate the analysis of 
large-scale datasets. Our goal is to accelerate the discovery process through 
accelerated algorithms and make the code, along with its associated scientific 
curiosity, accessible to the public. The project's website can be found at 
https://em-acc.org. The corresponding code, known as EMView, can be accessed at 
https://github.com/EMView/EMView.

This paper examines the problem of robot locomotion in soft or changing terrain conditions.
The main obstacle in mobile robot movement on unstable surfaces is determining the
robot's foot position on the ground, specifically when it contacts the ground or lifts
off. Existing methods for foot contact detection often rely on the use of force sensors,
which are prone to inaccuracies due to the uncertainty of foot-ground interaction forces.
To address this issue, we propose a new method that combines force information with
the robot's foot position to enhance contact determination. Our approach is tested on
a humanoid robot moving across a variety of soft terrain surfaces, including foam, snow,
and sand, and evaluated in comparison to established contact determination methods.
The results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method in improving contact
identification and reducing the uncertainty associated with soft landings. The code for
our research is available for open access at https://github.com/ctiemilo/ContactUncertainty. 
We anticipate that our findings will be useful for the development of robots capable of
moving across soft terrain. A video demonstrating our results can be accessed on
the YouTube platform: https://youtu.be/6ZJzg6zg6zg.

The primary objective of monocular 3D object detection is to identify a 3D bounding box for each object within a given image, utilizing depth information derived from the image, assuming a single, unidimensional depth channel is provided. The majority of existing methods rely on the assumption that objects within the scene share a common scale, which is often represented by the size of the image. However, this can be problematic, as objects within the scene may have varying scales, leading to suboptimal performance. In this study, a novel method called Scale-Aware Depth Module (SaD) is introduced to address this limitation. SaD is designed to incorporate depth information in a way that is independent of object scale, effectively allowing for the extraction of object size from the image. The proposed module is then integrated into the CenterPoint framework, which is a leading method in monocular 3D object detection, and tested on the KITTI benchmark. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, with a higher AP and lower ADE scores. Verified controller synthesis involves designing a control system that meets specific safety and task requirements. These requirements are often specified in mission-oriented scenarios using temporal logic rules that must be satisfied in all situations. Developing such systems is challenging because they need to operate in unpredictable environments where the full state is not always available, making it difficult to ensure safety and task completion. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach to create a simplified model of the world, called a symbolic environment model, which can be used to evaluate the safety and task requirements. This model is generated from real-world data and is utilized within a learning-based controller synthesis framework, enabling the design of control systems that can operate safely and efficiently in a variety of situations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments on complex robotic control tasks, which involve tasks such as tracking trajectories and navigating obstacle courses. The results show that our approach successfully synthesizes control systems that can meet the required specifications and perform well in both simulated and real-world settings. However, its performance in real-world applications remains uncertain, particularly when labelled data is scarce and class distributions are unevenly balanced. To address this, a comprehensive comparison of SSL and supervised learning in the context of imbalanced data is undertaken. Through a series of controlled experiments on two datasets, it is revealed that supervised learning significantly outperforms SSL when class imbalance is a factor, highlighting the need for further investigation into SSL's limitations in real-world applications. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that balancing class distributions can mitigate the performance gap between SSL and supervised learning, underscoring the importance of developing more robust SSL techniques that can effectively handle imbalanced data. To this end, a novel framework for self-supervised learning is proposed, incorporating a self-supervised balancing loss to iteratively rebalance class distributions during training. The framework is validated through a series of experiments, showing that it successfully addresses the imbalance issue and yields superior performance compared to existing methods. Ensuring the stability of model explanations is vital in high-stakes applications, but current methods fall short in addressing this requirement. These approaches either focus on local accuracy or rely on assumptions that may not hold in real-world scenarios, such as feature sparsity in tabular data. Consequently, explanations are vulnerable to minor changes in the data distribution, leading to potential misinterpretation. To address this issue, we introduce a robustness metric that assesses a method's stability by measuring the alignment between explanation and original features. We propose several metrics and demonstrate their efficacy with both simulated and real-world datasets, under various conditions that simulate shifts in the data distribution. Our results indicate that traditional metrics fail to capture stability effectively, while our proposed metrics provide a more accurate measure of explanation robustness. Furthermore, our experiments show that local accuracy assumptions can be significantly violated in practice, highlighting the need for model-agnostic metrics that can be applied across various explanation techniques. Overall, our research demonstrates the importance of considering explanation robustness in high-stakes settings and presents a novel approach for evaluating this aspect. A novel technique called Reinforced Dynamics (RiD) has been developed to efficiently explore energy landscapes by utilizing a personalized potential function that adapts to each system's characteristics. RiD employs machine learning to generate a unique potential for each state, allowing it to mimic the dynamics of the most likely state's transition. We have successfully applied and optimized RiD using a neural network for the first time, achieving impressive results. Our research demonstrates that RiD can effectively navigate high-dimensional energy landscapes by leveraging system-specific information and utilizing machine learning to enhance its capabilities. We have successfully applied this RiD approach to a complex biological system, using it to explore the conformational space of the apoferritin protein and identify the transition dynamics between its substates. Our findings show that RiD can accurately predict the equilibrium dynamics of this protein, even when it is subjected to different conditions. Furthermore, our results indicate that RiD can efficiently explore large conformational spaces, making it an ideal tool for studying protein folding and unfolding processes. We believe that RiD has great potential as a powerful tool for exploring complex energy landscapes in a variety of biological systems. Our results highlight the challenges of applying PINNs to a broader range of complex problems. To mitigate these issues, we suggest several strategies that can improve PINN performance, including incorporating boundary conditions and using more advanced architectures. Our work aims to raise awareness about the potential limitations of PINNs and stimulate further research into their use for solving ODEs. This research paper investigates the problem of simultaneous remote state estimation of multiple linear time-invariant systems while ensuring security and privacy. It assumes that multiple systems share the same state, which is influenced by unknown noise, and that each system must continuously estimate the states of all other systems as well as its own, despite being vulnerable to interception by an eavesdropper. To resolve this challenge, the study develops a secure estimation strategy that involves the exchange of encrypted data among the systems, using a distributed Kalman filter to estimate their individual states. To maintain confidentiality, the systems secretly agree on a set of shared encryption keys, used to encode and decode data before and after transmission. Crucially, the study proves that this approach yields the minimum mean square error bound for each system's state estimation, assuming the eavesdropper's capabilities are known. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that this approach is both feasible and scalable, as it can be applied to a large number of systems, and the secure estimation error is limited by the amount of data exchanged and the effectiveness of the encryption method. Finally, the study validates its approach with simulation results that confirm its performance. These results show that the secure estimation method closely approximates the optimal estimation method in the absence of eavesdroppers, and that it can effectively mitigate the impact of eavesdropping on the estimates. We have made our code publicly available for easy implementation. The related repository can be found at https://github.com/smartmornen/Distributed-Secure-Kalman-Filter. Structural seismic interpretation is a crucial step in understanding the Earth's structure, encompassing the identification of subsurface attributes such as geometry, depth, and rock properties. These features are vital for geologists to piece together the Earth's evolutionary history. Within the field of structural geology, a long-standing debate surrounds the impact of faulting mechanisms on fault block geometry. This debate has implications for seismic interpretation, as the correct identification of geometry influences not only the Earth's structural evolution but also the distribution of hydrocarbon reservoirs. This study presents a novel approach to seismic interpretation that incorporates a geometric model of faults, enabling the simultaneous estimation of rock properties and fault block geometry from seismic data. Using a probabilistic framework, our method allows for the generation of multiple possible interpretations of subsurface geometry. This is compared to existing work, highlighting key differences in our methodology and the benefits of considering geometry in seismic interpretation. A 2D and 3D synthetic example demonstrates the effectiveness of our method, which will be applied to real seismic data in future work. This research has significant potential to improve seismic interpretation, particularly in the field of hydrocarbon reservoirs, where the incorporation of geometric knowledge is expected to lead to more accurate reservoir estimates. The developed methodology is anticipated to be applied in other geophysical applications, such as imaging below ice sheets. The accompanying code and synthetic data are available at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/GeorgSue/GeometryBasedInterpretation. The objective of salient object detection is to identify and isolate the most visually prominent objects within an image. This task has been extensively researched in computer vision, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) emerging as the dominant method. However, existing CNN-based models often rely on manually designed pooling strategies that may lack adaptability to various image types. To address this limitation, a novel self-calculating feature learning approach, referred to as Global Context Co-occurrence (GCC), has been proposed. GCC leverages the global context and local object characteristics by dynamically fusing feature maps at different scales. Furthermore, a pixel-level confidence score is computed to refine the detection accuracy. To address the challenge of handling images with diverse backgrounds, a global confidence map is generated through a pixel-wise voting mechanism. Experimental evaluations on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, revealing superior performance compared to 19 state-of-the-art alternatives.
